title: Chelsea Thompto - Spaces for Contemplation: Procedural Generation in Nonlinear Narrative in Art
speaker: Chelsea Thompto
talk_title: Spaces for Contemplation: Procedural Generation in Nonlinear Narrative in Art
description: An artist talk about how procedural generation can be employed in a new media arts context to create spaces that have legible and concrete themes but that also resist linear narrative construction.

segments.text: Excellent. So next up is Chelsea Topto,
who is here to talk about
procedural generation and non-linear
narrative in art. I'll let you take it
away, Chelsea.
>> Thank you. And before I get started, I
just want to also say thank you to the
organizers. This is my first time
attending the event synchronously and
also my first time speaking, and I just
really appreciate all the work that goes
into it.
And I'd also just like to give two
little programming notes. The first is
that you're going to see moving images
throughout the presentation, but there
is no sound
in those moving images. So as long as
you're hearing my voice, you're getting
everything that is intended. And then
the last thing I'll say is that there is
a link to the slides which includes the
code that I talk about because today's
talk is going to be a little bit more
focused on the visual and conceptual
aspects and a little bit less on the
technical.
So as an artist, I'm drawn to creating
work about my specific political and
personal context as a trans woman.
But I have also always had an aversion
to my work being understood as being as
having one clear, simplistic message or
becoming another site of
objectification.
So I create systems that resist linear
narrative readings in favor of creating
spaces of contemplation
populated with the texts, visual forms,
and feelings I want the viewer to
confront.
This talk will be a brief examination of
this process and of how procedural
generation can be employed in a new
media and book arts context to create
spaces that have legible and concrete
themes, but that also resist
narrative, linear narrative
construction.
So the heart of this work for me is the
question, how might procedural
generation be used in art to address
specific political struggles, while also
resisting the context of asymmetrical
visibility that has caused harm to so
many minoritized communities.
So I want to talk a little bit about um
two sets of influences. First, Vera
Molnár and Sol LeWitt from the fine art
standpoint. Um I'm trained as a visual
artist, trained in um sculpture and
drawing. And so these artists were some
of my first introductions to
randomization and procedural generation.
And they really allowed me to understand
that uh a single drop of randomization
can be extremely powerful in a work of
art and that you actually don't need a
huge amount of random number generation
to create um pretty stunning and
interesting things.
Um and as an artist, uh I've also been a
lifelong um gamer. And uh for me, there
was a long period of time where I didn't
have access to any console games. Uh and
so games like Ancient Domains of
Mystery, um NetHack, and other roguelike
games which which I didn't even really
fully understand as a genre um were
really my main touch point for games. Um
and of course uh contemporary work also
uh influences my thinking.
So I want to start with the work um
titled Productive Bodies.
Uh so Productive Bodies is a non-linear
single channel video. The piece overlays
videos of the Mississippi River, river
maps, and renderings of gender-affirming
surgical techniques to create a living
Xerox effect.
So that effect can be seen here.
So in this work, um this is one of the
first times I was really able to think
through randomization or procedural
generation as something that could be
useful in my artwork. Um this is powered
by um Java in the um
library called Processing, um which is
really popular with artists and
designers. And this work overlays um
undulating uh
video of the Mississippi River, which I
took at its headwaters, um with maps of
the Mississippi River and renderings of
um
medical procedures often associated with
gender-affirming care. Uh all of this is
sort of po- posterized and then given
this tint, which creates this sort of
undulating um
scene that you see before you. So the
work draws from over 50 different media
sources. So at any given point, I
understand that a viewer is going to see
the river, a map of the river, and these
medical procedures. But what exactly is
interacting with one another and how
they're interacting is unpredictable.
And that's what I mean by a space of
contemplation, a space where I am
thinking about and designing
relationships rather than a specific
narrative.
So I took this idea that I made with
code and I started to think about how uh
it might be represented in a physical
form, which led me to the question, what
would a book look like if the spine was
a point rather than a line?
This led me to design a physical
node-based spine structure for a book.
You can see it here.
And to actually print that and create a
functioning, non-linear, nodal-based
book that mimicked the non-linear ideas
that I was working in the code.
Uh you can see one installation version
of it here.
And this really became a core part of my
practice, this idea of thinking about
creating spaces of relationship
digitally and then also thinking about
ways to work that into physical
manifestations.
And all along the way here, I'm really
thinking pretty broadly about procedural
generation, but in particular, you know,
I'm really interested in not necessarily
what technical process, but rather how
that result is manifest in a viewer.
So I'm going to move on now to the fog.
Um this piece, the fog, and the last
piece I'm going to talk about, A Walk in
the Dark, were both created um primarily
with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript um using
the Three.js library for the 3D effects
that you'll see.
So the fog is a web experience in three
acts. Each act features a 3D scene with
a different camera/control scheme.
The scenes draw from archival and
artist-authored text which are used um
in the generated spaces.
So here we actually see the contents
page and the first really basic use of
procedural generation in the sort of
title card that comes up. Every time the
page is refreshed, a new version of this
wall of fog text comes up. And one of
the really exciting things about this
work is um it was commissioned through a
museum and so we're really interested in
thinking about accessibility. And so I
was able to
tie in the ARIA tag system in JavaScript
and um
web pages in general to make it so that
a screen reader would ignore all of the
symbol text and only pull out um the
physical the actual text that you can
read, the readable text um for screen
readers. And so it was also a chance for
me to think about how procedural
generation can spread out into these
accessibility technologies.
The works themselves are all comprised
of 3D spaces again created with
Three.js. Um these spaces are all
rendered uh live on the screen with
ASCII characters rather than with uh
say, you know, regular rendering
geometry that you might see on the web.
This causes the uh physicality, the
materiality of the space to be really
obvious. Um I'm really interested in
thinking about digital materiality and
um not really allowing the
myth of like a perfect virtual world to
to take hold. And so I'm like I'm always
trying to find ways to sort of undercut
immersion in some way or um
verisimilitude to reality in some way uh
in favor of creating immersion of an
idea, of a concept, of a set of
relationships. So um finally with the
fog piece I want to talk about how this
piece became physicalized. So I pulled
um parts of this out, the text portions
of this out, and I created these
inverted fog lights. And so these fog
lights have textured glass. It's a small
Raspberry Pi that um runs a little live
web page that feeds um from a large body
of text and displays them on the screen.
The screens do not really emit light as
much as they require someone to lean
into them. And so
what I really love about this work is
that a fog light, which is usually meant
to pierce through
um the veil of fog, is instead here uh
inviting people to peer in.
So the last work I want to talk about is
my current ongoing piece uh a walk in
the dark.
So this piece is a piece composed of six
poems, each with six lines. The poems
are displayed across a variety of
repeating spaces. When one poem ends,
the other is random another is randomly
chosen, and the spaces are shuffled and
reordered. So here I'm thinking about
randomization and authorship and how I
can bring those two things together in a
balance. Again, in all of this work, I'm
really interested in thinking about ways
that I myself as a trans woman um or
other minoritized people can actually
speak their stories and their truth
without necessarily coming into contact
with the idea of trauma porn or having
their work and their ideas and their
were sort of consumed for melodramatic
content. And for me, I think procedural
generation is a lovely way to sort of
flip the script on what we normally
think of as narrative and also to insist
upon viewers sitting with a work for a
longer period of time. This for me is
one of the things I love about the
roguelike genre in general is that a
work kind of blossoms and grows in one's
mind over time and in over experiencing
it um rather than being immediately uh
clear what the work totally is and what
it's about.
So in this uh scene here, you can see
the uh
piece as it's functioning. Um it is
inspired by tunnel books. Tunnel books
are books that have accordion sides that
you look through the front. And so my
idea was how could you make a shuffling,
randomizing tunnel book that would um
shuffle the scenes over time and feed
the lines of poems scene by scene.
This has led to me looking at historical
examples of tunnel books
and finally has led to me figuring out
how to create a procedurally generated
physical tunnel book. Um so I'm thinking
about how one might need to roll dice or
otherwise determine the order uh and
thinking about how these ideas of
procedural generation and randomization
can again take physical form.
Um so I'll end it there. Again, the QR
code at the top is a link to the slides
um and some of the pieces I talked about
here are represented um in the links.
Thank you very much.
>> Thank you. That's wonderful. Um yeah,
the tunnel box. That's that's beautiful,
the tunnel book. Um

Um,

Do you discard a lot of designs as

>> Yeah, so um I'll say again I'm trained
as more of a sculptor and I started
coding um as a self-taught person in
2016 or so um with the prompting of of a
professor who was like maybe try this
and then kind of let me uh go. And and
so yeah, for me I find I plan a lot in
sketchbooks and I have an idea. Um, like
for this piece this last piece it's like
what would a tunnel book look like on
the internet? And that is sort of the
plan and then from there I'm building.
Um, I've in the last like six years I've
really kind of leaned into 3JS. So a lot
of my design patterns and thinking go
into that just because it's like the
thing that I'm learning. But I'm
currently learning um a new software
which is L5 which is processing for Lua.
Uh, so I'm not familiar with the Lua
programming language before starting
this. Um, but it is starting to produce
like new patterns in my brain. So it is
a it is sort of a dynamic process
between like what is visually and
conceptually interesting and then like
how would I um make that happen
technically, and then that technical
execution always changes and informs the
work in ways that I find really
exciting.
>> Cool. Yeah, thank you. I think that's
one thing that yeah speaks to a lot of

process is itself part of what feeds
into the artistic process. So,
excellent. Well, thank you so much and
uh yeah hopefully people can do some
follow-up in the breakout rooms, but uh
it was wonderful to have you at
Roguelike Celebration. Thank you so much
